pages.title: Array Initialization in Java
pages.content:
In Java, **array initialization** allocates memory on the JVM heap and assigns initial values to the array elements.

### Three Ways to Initialize an Array in Java

#### 1. Dynamic Allocation (Default Values)
Specify the size using the `new` keyword. The JVM allocates contiguous memory and populates elements with default values:
```java
int[] numbers = new int[5]; // Creates array of size 5 with default 0s: [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
```

#### 2. Static Initialization (Direct Initialization)
When values are known in advance, initialize directly using curly braces:
```java
int[] primes = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11}; // Compiler determines size = 5 automatically
```

#### 3. Anonymous Array Initialization
Useful when passing a newly created array directly into a method without declaring a separate variable:
```java
printScores(new int[]{95, 88, 72, 90});
```

### Memory Architecture of Arrays
```default
Stack (Reference)              Heap (Contiguous Memory Block)
+---------------+              +----+----+----+----+----+
| numbers       | ---------->  | 0  | 1  | 2  | 3  | 4  |  <- Indices
+---------------+              +----+----+----+----+----+
                               | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 |  <- Stored Values
                               +----+----+----+----+----+
```

> [!NOTE]
> Arrays in Java are **fixed-length objects**. Once created, their length cannot be modified. To change capacity, you must allocate a new array and copy elements over.

pages.title: Accessing Array Elements
pages.content:
- Alright! Since you already know how to declare and initialize an array, let’s move on to how you can **access the values stored inside it**.
- Think of an array like a **row of lockers**, and each locker has a number (called an **index**) starting from 0.

So if you have this array:

```java
int[] numbers = {5, 10, 15, 20, 25};
```

You can think of it like this:

```java
Index: 0 1 2 3 4
Value: 5 10 15 20 25
```

To get a specific value, you just need to use its **index**.

---

**Syntax**

```java
arrayName[index];
```
---

**Example**
```java
class Seedit {
 public static void main(String[] args) {
 int[] numbers = {5, 10, 15, 20, 25}; // Indexes are 0,1,2,3,4

 System.out.println("First element: " + numbers[0]); // Output: 5
 System.out.println("Third element: " + numbers[2]); // Output: 15
 System.out.println("Last element: " + numbers[4]); // Output: 25
 System.out.println("Last element: " + numbers[5]); // ERROR: No such index
 }
}
```

pages.title: Adding Elements at a Specific Index in ArrayList
pages.content:
In our previous lessons, we learned how to declare, initialize, access, and update elements in an ArrayList. Now, we'll learn how to add an element at a specific position using the `add(int index, E element)` method.

The `add(int index, E element)` method allows you to:
1. Insert an element at any valid position in the ArrayList
2. Shift all existing elements after that position to the right

---

Example:
```java
ArrayList fruits = new ArrayList<>();
fruits.add("Apple"); // ["Apple"]
fruits.add("Banana"); // ["Apple", "Banana"]
fruits.add(1, "Mango"); // ["Apple", "Mango", "Banana"]
```

- The index must be between 0 and the current size of the ArrayList (inclusive)
- Trying to add at an invalid index (like index 5 in a 3-element list) will throw an IndexOutOfBoundsException
- This is different from the simple add() method we learned earlier which always adds at the end

options: It is shifted to index 2 along with all subsequent elements
It is permanently overwritten and replaced by "X"
It is deleted from the list
checkpoint.explanation: add(index, element) is an insertion operation. Elements at and above the target index shift one position to the right.

pages.title: Checking if an Element Exists in an ArrayList
pages.content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to check whether a specific element exists in an ArrayList using the `contains(value)` method.

---

The `contains()` method is very simple:
- It takes one parameter: the object you want to check for
- It returns `true` if the element exists in the ArrayList
- It returns `false` if the element doesn't exist

For example, if we have an ArrayList of fruits:
```java
ArrayList fruits = new ArrayList<>();
fruits.add("Apple");
fruits.add("Banana");
fruits.add("Orange");
```

We can check if "Banana" exists:
```java
boolean hasBanana = fruits.contains("Banana"); // returns true
boolean hasGrape = fruits.contains("Grape"); // returns false
boolean hasBanana = fruits.contains("banana"); // returns false because the check is case-sensitive for Strings
```

pages.title: isEmpty() Method in ArrayList
pages.content:
- The `isEmpty()` method in ArrayList is a simple and useful way to check if your ArrayList has any elements or not.
- It returns `true` if the ArrayList is empty (has no elements) and `false` if it contains one or more elements.

---

**Example:**
```java
ArrayList fruits = new ArrayList<>();
System.out.println(fruits.isEmpty()); // Output: true
fruits.add("Apple");
System.out.println(fruits.isEmpty()); // Output: false because ArrayList has the size 1
```

pages.title: Why ArrayList?
pages.content:
A Java array has a fixed length. `ArrayList` is a resizable collection that is useful when the number of elements changes while the program runs.

Think of an `ArrayList<Integer>` as a sequence with indexes:
`0, 1, 2, ... size-1`.

Core operations:
- `add(x)` → append
- `add(index, x)` → insert
- `get(index)` → read
- `set(index, x)` → replace
- `remove(index)` → remove by position
- `size()` → number of elements

Important: `size()` is a method; it is not a field like array `length`.

pages.title: Indexing, get, and set
pages.content:
ArrayList indexes start at 0, just like arrays. For `[10, 20, 30]`, `get(0)` is 10 and `get(2)` is 30.

`set(index, value)` changes an existing element; it does not increase the list size.

Example:
`[10, 20, 30]`
`set(1, 99)` → `[10, 99, 30]`

An invalid index causes `IndexOutOfBoundsException`. Before accessing `i`, ensure `0 <= i < list.size()`.

callout.title: Key concept

checkpoint.explanation: The set() method replaces the existing element at the given index without changing list size.

pages.title: Traversing an ArrayList
pages.content:
Use an indexed loop when you need positions; use an enhanced for-loop when you only need values.

For `[4, 7, 2]`:
```text
indexed: i=0 → 4, i=1 → 7, i=2 → 2
for-each: x=4 → x=7 → x=2
```

A common beginner mistake is using `i <= list.size()`; the final valid index is `size()-1`, so the condition must be `i < list.size()`.

callout.title: Key concept
callout.text: The largest valid index is one less than the size, so `i < size` visits every element exactly once.

checkpoint.question: Which loop condition is correct for iterating through indices 0 to size - 1 of an ArrayList?
checkpoint.explanation: Because valid indices run from 0 to list.size() - 1, the condition i < list.size() ensures every element is visited exactly once.

Using your current knowledge of arrays - you can solve the following problem!
### Task

It's the soccer match finals in Chefland and as always it has reached the penalty shootouts.
- Each team is given $5$ shots to make and the team scoring a goal on the maximum number of shots wins the game.
- If both the teams' scores are equal, then the game is considered a draw and we would have $2$ champions.

Given ten integers $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_{10}$, determine the winner or find if the game ends in a draw. 
- the odd indexed integers($A_1, A_3,$ $A_5,$ $A_7, A_9$) represent the outcome of the shots made by team $1$
- the even indexed integers($A_2, A_4, A_6, A_8, A_{10}$) represent the outcome of the shots made by team $2$ 

Note that here $A_i = 1$ indicates that it's a goal and $A_i = 0$ indicates a miss.

practiceProblems.description:
Alice has an array of $N$ integers — $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_N$.\
She wants the product of all the elements of the array to be a non-negative integer. \
That is, it can be either $0$ or positive. But she doesn't want it to be negative.

To do this, she is willing to remove some elements of the array. \
Determine the  minimum number of elements that she will have to remove to make the product of the array's elements non-negative.

topics.description: Master the most-used ArrayList operations and understand the subtle difference between searching, removing, inserting, copying, and clearing.

pages.title: Search with contains and indexOf
pages.content:
`contains(value)` answers whether a value exists. `indexOf(value)` returns the first index, or `-1` when the value is absent.

Example:
`[10, 20, 10, 30]`
- `contains(20)` → true
- `indexOf(10)` → 0
- `indexOf(30)` → 3
- `indexOf(99)` → -1

If you need every matching position, scan the list yourself.

callout.title: Key concept
callout.text: Understand the rule, trace a small example by hand, then implement it in Java.

codeCard.code:
ArrayList<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(10, 20, 10, 30));
System.out.println(a.contains(20)); // true
System.out.println(a.indexOf(10));   // 0
System.out.println(a.indexOf(99));   // -1

checkpoint.question: Given ArrayList list = [10, 20, 10, 30], what is returned by list.indexOf(10) and list.indexOf(99)?
options: indexOf(10) returns 0; indexOf(99) throws an exception
checkpoint.explanation: indexOf() returns the first index of the matching element (index 0 for 10), and returns -1 if the element is not found.

pages.title: Remove: index vs value
pages.content:
`remove` has an important Java overload for `ArrayList<Integer>`:
- `remove(int index)` removes by position.
- `remove(Integer value)` removes the first matching value.

Therefore `list.remove(2)` on an `ArrayList<Integer>` removes index 2, not the value 2.

To remove the value 2 explicitly, use `list.remove(Integer.valueOf(2))`.

callout.text: Understand the rule, trace a small example by hand, then implement it in Java.

checkpoint.question: Why is 'list.remove(Integer.valueOf(2))' necessary when removing the number 2 from an ArrayList<Integer>?
options: It invokes the remove(Object o) overload instead of the remove(int index) overload
It converts the ArrayList into a HashSet
It removes all occurrences of 2 simultaneously
It sorts the list before removal
checkpoint.explanation: Passing an int literal (2) matches the remove(int index) method. Wrapping 2 in Integer.valueOf(2) ensures remove(Object o) is called.

pages.title: Insert, clear, and copy
pages.content:
`add(index, value)` shifts later elements to the right. `clear()` removes all elements.

For copying, `new ArrayList<>(oldList)` creates a separate list containing the current elements. Assigning `copy = oldList` only creates another reference to the same list.

This distinction matters when a problem requires an independent result.

pages.title: Complexity intuition
pages.content:
For beginner-level DSA, you should know the usual cost of common operations.

- `get(i)`: typically O(1)
- `set(i,x)`: O(1)
- `add(x)` at the end: amortized O(1)
- `contains(x)`: O(N)
- `indexOf(x)`: O(N)
- insert/remove near the beginning or middle: O(N) because elements may shift

This explains why repeated insertion at index 0 can become slow for a large list.

callout.title: Key concept
callout.text: Searching is linear in the worst case because the target may be at the end or absent.

checkpoint.explanation: Inserting at the beginning requires shifting all N elements right by one position, taking linear O(N) time.

pages.title: Filtering an ArrayList
pages.content:
A common DSA task is: “keep only the values satisfying a condition.”

Beginner-friendly approach: create a new list and scan the original. For `[3, 8, 2, 9]`, keeping values greater than 5 gives `[8, 9]`.

This is often clearer and safer than removing elements from the same list while traversing it.

pages.title: Conditional removal
pages.content:
If you must remove matching elements, an index-based loop can work by moving from right to left. Removing index `i` does not change the indexes of elements before `i`.

Example: remove all even values from `[2, 5, 8, 9]`.
Scan from the end:
- remove 8
- remove 2
Result: `[5, 9]`

This avoids accidentally skipping an element after a left-to-right removal.

checkpoint.question: When removing all even values from an ArrayList of Integers using an index loop, why is right-to-left traversal safe?
options: Removing index i shifts elements to the right of i, leaving elements with indices < i untouched
It automatically reverses the order of elements
It prevents garbage collection during removal
Right-to-left loops run twice as fast
checkpoint.explanation: Because elements shift left into index i, indices lower than i are completely unaffected, so a countdown loop never misses an item.

pages.title: Frequency without advanced data structures
pages.content:
Before learning maps, you can solve small frequency tasks by scanning.

Example: count how many times 4 occurs in `[4, 1, 4, 7, 4]`.
Start `count=0`; increment whenever the current value equals 4. Result = 3.

This teaches an important general pattern: **scan + condition + accumulator**.
Later, a `HashMap` will make “count every distinct value” more efficient for large inputs.

pages.title: Choose Array vs ArrayList
pages.content:
Use an **array** when:
- the number of elements is fixed or known,
- direct primitive storage matters,
- you want simple indexed storage.

Use **ArrayList** when:
- the number of elements can grow/shrink,
- you need convenient collection operations,
- object types are acceptable (`Integer`, `Long`, etc.).

Neither is universally “better”. Choose based on the problem's requirements.

practiceProblems.title: Review problem - 4
practiceProblems.description:
Abhi is a salesman. He was given two types of candies, which he is selling in $N$ different cities.

For the prices of the candies to be valid, Abhi's boss laid down the following condition:
- A given type of candy must have **distinct** prices in all $N$ cities.

In his excitement, Abhi wrote down the prices of both the candies on the same page and in random order instead of writing them on different pages. Now he is asking for your help to find out if the prices he wrote are valid or not.

More formally, you are given an array $A$ of size $2N$. Find out whether it is possible to split $A$ into two arrays, each of length $N$, such that both arrays consist of distinct elements.
